design-controls-s1.title: The grease-spot test
design-controls-s1.text: Fats and oils (lipids) are hydrophobic: they soak into paper and do not evaporate, leaving a see-through (translucent) spot. Water also makes paper see-through, but only until it evaporates. A class rubbed each sample onto brown paper, waited 30 minutes, then held the paper up to a light.

table.caption: Grease-spot results after 30 minutes of drying

design-controls-s2.title: A starch test that went wrong
design-controls-s2.text: Iodine solution turns blue-black when it meets starch and stays orange-brown otherwise. A student added three drops of iodine to each test tube below. All tubes were rinsed in the same tub of wash water before use.

table.caption: Color of each tube after adding iodine

items.q: Which sample is the negative control, and what possibility does it rule out?
options: Distilled water; it rules out that the paper or the procedure makes a lasting spot without any fat.
Vegetable oil; it rules out that the test fails to detect fat on this paper on this day.
Apple slice; it rules out that foods from plants contain fat, since apples come from plants.
Distilled water; it rules out that the foods were contaminated with extra water before the test began on the paper.

why.correct: A negative control should give no response. Water is treated exactly like the foods. Because it leaves no spot after 30 minutes, any lasting spot from a food cannot be blamed on wetness, the paper or the handling.
options: Correct: expected negative, treated identically, rules out a false positive from the method.
Oil is the positive control; it rules out a false negative.
The apple is a test sample, not a control, and its result says nothing about other plant foods.
Water is the right sample, but it rules out a spot made by the method, not water in the foods.

items.q: Suppose the vegetable oil had left no spot. What could the class conclude about the apple's "No" result?
options: Nothing reliable: the test failed to detect a known fat, so the apple could contain fat that was missed.
The apple contains no fat, because its result matches the result for the vegetable oil.
The apple contains more fat than the oil, because neither of them left a spot on the paper.
The apple contains no fat, because the water also left no spot, which shows that the negative control worked properly.

why.correct: The positive control checks that the test can give a "yes". If a known fat gives "no", the test is not working today (wrong paper, too little sample, wiped off), so other "no" results cannot be trusted.
options: Correct: a failed positive control makes negatives untrustworthy.
Matching a failed positive control shows the test is broken, not that the apple lacks fat.
Two blank results give no basis for ranking fat content.
A working negative control rules out false positives; it does nothing to rule out false negatives.

items.q: A student checks the paper after 2 minutes instead of 30 and records "Yes" for the apple slice. What most likely explains this result?
options: The apple's juice, which is mostly water, had not yet evaporated, so wetness made a spot that would have faded.
The apple contains a large amount of fat, which slowly evaporates from the paper over the 30 minutes.
Water is hydrophobic, so the apple's water soaked into the paper and stayed there like an oil would.
Checking early made the test more sensitive, so the "Yes" at 2 minutes is the correct reading for the apple.

why.correct: Water also makes paper translucent until it evaporates. Wetness is a factor that differs between juicy and dry foods, so reading early lets it produce a false positive. The 30-minute wait, checked by the water control, removes it.
options: Correct: a temporary water spot, a false positive.
Fats do not evaporate at room temperature; that is why their spot lasts.
Water is polar and evaporates; lipids are the hydrophobic ones that stay.
Reading early adds false positives from water; the water control shows spots must last 30 minutes to count.

items.q: Which claim about the unknown powder is best supported, given both controls behaved as expected?
options: The powder probably contains some fat, but less than the peanut, because its spot was faint rather than large.
The powder contains no fat, because a faint spot is closer to the water result than it is to the large spot made by the oil.
The powder is pure fat, because a lasting spot means the sample is made of lipid alone.
Nothing can be said, because the powder was not tested alongside a positive control.

why.correct: With water blank and oil positive, a lasting faint spot points to a small amount of fat. The test is rough, so "less than the peanut" is as far as it goes.
options: Correct: a cautious claim matched to a cautious test.
A lasting spot, however faint, is a positive result once the water control shows the method makes none.
A faint spot suggests a little fat, not a sample that is all fat.
The oil positive control was run in the same session, so it covers the powder too.

items.q: Which result shows that the experiment has a problem?
options: Tube 2, because distilled water should stay orange-brown with iodine.
Tube 1, because starch solution should stay orange-brown with iodine.
Tube 3, because potato extract is expected to be free of starch.
Tube 5, because vegetable oil should turn fully blue-black.

why.correct: Distilled water is the negative control. It has no starch, so it should stay orange-brown. A blue-black result means starch got in from somewhere.
options: Correct: the negative control failed.
Starch solution is the positive control; blue-black is the expected result.
Potatoes store a lot of starch; blue-black is expected.
Oil is a lipid, not starch; it is not expected to turn blue-black.

items.q: What is the most likely cause of the blue-black color in the tubes of distilled water and sugar water?
options: Starch carried over in the shared wash water coated every tube, contaminating them before the samples went in.
Table sugar is a polysaccharide made of glucose, so it reacts with iodine just as starch does.
Iodine turns blue-black on its own after several minutes in a tube, whether or not starch is present in the solution.
Distilled water breaks down into starch when iodine is added, by dehydration synthesis of water molecules.

why.correct: Every tube was rinsed in the same tub. Starch from the starch-solution tube or potato extract in that water would coat each tube, so even water and sugar test positive. The failed negative control reveals the contamination.
options: Correct: a shared source of starch explains positives in tubes that should be negative.
Table sugar is sucrose, a disaccharide (glucose + fructose), not a polysaccharide; it does not give the starch color.
If iodine alone turned blue-black, it would be useless as a starch test; the positive and negative colors differ.
Water does not turn into starch; dehydration synthesis joins monomers such as glucose and needs them to be present.

items.q: What should the student do next?
options: Repeat the whole test with new, separately rinsed tubes, including both controls.
Keep the results for tubes 3 and 5, since those are the foods of real interest here.
Drop tube 2 from the report, since a control is not part of the actual results.
Report that sugar contains starch, since tube 4 turned the same color as tube 1.

why.correct: A failed negative control means every result may be a false positive. The fix is to remove the cause (shared wash water) and rerun everything with both controls.
options: Correct: remove the cause, repeat with controls.
If the tubes were contaminated, the food results are untrustworthy too.
Hiding a failed control hides the problem; the control is what reveals it.
Tube 4 is explained by contamination, so it is not evidence that sugar contains starch.

items.q: In this experiment, what role does tube 1 (starch solution) play?
options: Positive control: it shows the iodine can detect starch.
Negative control: it shows what a starch-free tube looks like.
Independent variable: it is the factor the student changed.
Test sample: it is one of the foods being identified.

why.correct: A sample known to contain starch should turn blue-black; it confirms the iodine is working.
options: Correct.
The negative control is distilled water, which lacks starch.
The independent variable is the type of sample, not one tube.
Starch solution is a known reference, not an unknown food.

items.q: A student tests whether saturated fats melt at higher temperatures than unsaturated fats. She buys butter from one store and olive oil from another, and heats each in a different pan on a different stove. Which factor is most likely to be confounding?
options: The pans and stoves heat at different speeds, which could change the measured melting point.
The type of fat, because saturated and unsaturated fats differ in their structure.
The temperature at which each fat melts, which the student reads off a thermometer.
The stores where the fats were bought, because one of them sells more expensive brands.

why.correct: A confounding factor differs between groups and could affect the dependent variable. Different pans and stoves change how heat reaches each fat and how the temperature is read, so a difference could come from them rather than from the type of fat.
options: Correct: it differs between groups and plausibly affects the result.
Type of fat is the independent variable, the factor being tested.
Melting temperature is the dependent variable, the measured result.
Price differs, but price has no plausible effect on melting point; a confounding factor must also be able to change the result.

items.q: A test for fat uses a red dye that dissolves into lipids and colors them. Select ALL samples that would make a good positive control.
options: Vegetable oil
Distilled water
The red dye dissolved in water
Table sugar dissolved in water
The unknown food being tested

why.correct: A positive control is a sample known to contain what the test detects. Of these, only vegetable oil is a known fat.
options: Correct: a known fat.
Water has no lipid; it is a negative control.
Dye in water contains no lipid, so it shows nothing about whether the dye can color fat.
Sugar water is a carbohydrate solution with no fat; another negative.
An unknown cannot be a control, because its result is what you are trying to find out.

items.q: An exam answer says: "The control is the tube of water, because it is the control." Which addition would best earn the point for justifying the control?
options: "…because water contains no starch, so if it stays orange-brown, color changes in the food tubes are not caused by the tubes or the iodine."
"…because water is the standard control in most biology experiments, so the teacher will expect to see a water tube listed in the data table."
"…because water is a clear liquid, so it is easy to see whether the color of the iodine changes."
"…because the control has to be kept the same as the other tubes, so it should contain nothing of its own."

why.correct: Justifying a control means saying what it rules out: water lacks starch, so a negative result there shows the materials and method do not create a positive by themselves.
options: Correct: names what the control rules out.
Habit is not a reason, and water is not the right control for every test.
Easy visibility is convenient, but it says nothing about what the control rules out.
The control differs from the test tubes in exactly one respect (no sample), and this answer does not say what that shows.

items.q: To test whether a new paper detects fat more reliably than ordinary brown paper, a student uses peanut on both papers. What is the best negative control?
options: Distilled water rubbed onto both kinds of paper in the same way
Vegetable oil rubbed onto both kinds of paper in the same way
Peanut rubbed onto the new paper and read after 2 minutes
A blank sheet of each paper that is left untouched on the bench

why.correct: Water treated the same way checks that neither paper produces a lasting spot from the handling or from moisture.
options: Correct: same handling, no fat, both papers.
Oil is a known fat: a positive control.
Changing the reading time adds a second difference; it is not a control.
An untouched sheet skips the rubbing and wetting, so it would not reveal a spot made by the procedure.

items.q: What does a positive control rule out?
options: That a negative result happened because the test was not working
That a positive result happened because of contamination
That the independent variable was changed between groups
That repeated trials gave different results by chance

why.correct: A positive control is known to give the response, so it shows the test can detect it under the conditions used.
options: Correct: it rules out false negatives.
That is the job of a negative control (false positives).
Changing the independent variable is the point of the experiment.
Repeats deal with chance variation, not a control.

items.q: Two groups compared how much fat is in two brands of chips by weighing the grease spot each made. Group 1 used 5.0 g of brand X; group 2 used 2.0 g of brand Y and read the paper an hour later. Select ALL factors that are confounding.
options: Mass of chips used
Time before the paper was read
Brand of chips
Mass of the grease spot
Type of brown paper used by both groups

why.correct: Both mass of sample and reading time differ between the groups and could change the grease spot, so a difference cannot be credited to brand alone.
options: Confounding: more chips make a bigger spot regardless of brand.
Confounding: reading later lets water spots fade, changing what counts.
Brand is the independent variable, the factor being compared.
Spot mass is the dependent variable, the measured result.
The paper is the same for both groups, so it is controlled.

items.q: In a new run of the grease-spot test, the water leaves a lasting see-through spot and so does every food. Which explanation, if true, would account for both results?
options: The water bottle had a film of oil from an unwashed funnel, so every sample carried some lipid.
The foods contained more fat than usual, because they were bought from a different store this time.
The paper was too thin, so it could not show spots from any sample, including the oil.
Water is a lipid in small amounts, which is why water spots can last on brown paper.

why.correct: A failed negative control means something other than the sample is making the response. An oil film in the water would put lipid on every spot, including the water control.
options: Correct: contamination explains the failed negative control and the universal positives.
Fattier foods would not explain the water spot.
This predicts no spots at all, the opposite of what was seen.
Water is not a lipid; it evaporates from paper.
